S&P 500 daily price data fetched via yfinance (^GSPC, cached locally at

the same data. As-of **2026-06-16**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 daily (^GSPC, price return) | 1950-01-04 – 2023-12-29 | 18,618 trading days | `50dd18377a21` |
| World Cup windows | 19 editions (1950–2022) | 340 WC-window days / 351 control days | hardcoded constant |

## The Edmans et al. hypothesis

Edmans, Garcia & Norli (2007) show that football losses are associated with
negative **next-day** returns in the losing country. The global/S&P 500 version
tested here asks: does the S&P 500 systematically underperform during the
~32-trading-day World Cup window, across 19 tournaments?

## Per-window returns (bps/day)

| Edition | Host | n days | Mean return (bps/day) |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 1950 | Brazil | 14 | **-87.9** |
| 1954 | Switzerland | 13 | +20.2 |
| 1958 | Sweden | 15 | +4.1 |
| 1962 | Chile | 12 | **-30.2** |
| 1966 | England | 15 | **-31.0** |
| 1970 | Mexico | 15 | +4.9 |
| 1974 | West Germany | 16 | **-59.3** |
| 1978 | Argentina | 17 | -8.2 |
| 1982 | Spain | 19 | -11.2 |
| 1986 | Mexico | 20 | +4.9 |
| 1990 | Italy | 20 | -6.2 |
| 1994 | United States | 20 | -8.3 |
| 1998 | France | 22 | +18.7 |
| 2002 | South Korea/Japan | 21 | **-33.8** |
| 2006 | Germany | 20 | +3.4 |
| 2010 | South Africa | 20 | -3.3 |
| 2014 | Brazil | 21 | +5.9 |
| 2018 | Russia | 21 | +4.6 |
| 2022 | Qatar | 19 | -14.4 |
| **Overall** | | **340** | **-10.3** |

Key observation: 11 of 19 windows have negative mean returns. But the four
largest negative episodes (1950, 1974, 2002, 1966) coincide with known macro
crises: Korean War outbreak (June 25, 1950 — the S&P dropped ~15% in the WC
window due entirely to the war, not football), the 1973–74 oil crisis,
the dot-com bust (2002), and 1966 is a contested year. These confounds
dominate the signal.

## Statistical tests

### Primary test: per-edition mean return vs unconditional daily mean

The correct inference unit is the **19 independent tournaments**, not the
~340 pooled daily observations (which inflate effective n due to within-window
autocorrelation).

| Test | Statistic | p-value |
|---|---|---|
| Unconditional daily mean (full 1950–2023) | +3.53 bps/day | — |
| Mean WC-window daily return | **-10.3 bps/day** | — |
| Per-edition t-test (H₀: μ_WC = unconditional) | t = **-2.52** | **0.022** |
| Per-edition t-test (H₀: μ_WC = 0) | t = **-1.94** | **0.068** |
| Permutation test (two-sided, 10,000 shuffles) | — | **0.012** |

### Secondary test: WC days vs matched control windows

For each World Cup, we compare returns to a 2-years-prior same-season window
of identical duration.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean WC window | -10.3 bps/day |
| Mean matched control | +6.1 bps/day |
| Difference | **-16.4 bps/day** |
| Welch t (pooled WC days vs pooled control days) | t = **-2.29**, p = **0.022** |

### Binomial test: fraction of WC windows with negative mean

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| WC windows with negative mean | 11/19 (57.9%) |
| Binomial p (H₀: 50% negative) | p = **0.32** — not significant |

## Why this is not a tradable signal

1. **Confounds dominate.** The 1950 window coincides with the Korean War
   outbreak. The 1974 window with the oil crisis. The 2002 window with the
   dot-com bust. Drop these three outliers and the effect shrinks substantially.

2. **n = 19 is fragile.** With only 19 tournaments, one or two outliers
   determine the result. The per-edition standard deviation of WC window
   returns is ~25 bps/day — enormous relative to the -10.3 bps/day mean.

3. **No implementation vehicle.** "Go to cash every June-July when there's a
   World Cup" means being out of the market for ~5 weeks every 4 years (~3% of
   calendar time). The unconditional S&P return during non-WC periods is
   +3.8 bps/day; missing those also when the WC window turns positive costs you.

4. **Seasonal confounds.** World Cups are overwhelmingly held in summer
   (June–July), when US equity volumes are seasonally lower ("sell in May").
   The 2022 Qatar WC (November–December) had a -14.4 bps/day return, also
   coinciding with the rate-hike panic — not football sentiment.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The per-edition t-test vs the unconditional mean gives
  t = -2.52, p = 0.022 with n = 19, narrowly clearing the |t| >= 2 bar.
  However, the result is dominated by macro-crisis confounds (Korean War 1950,
  oil shock 1974, dot-com 2002), the binomial hit-rate is not significant
  (11/19 negative, p = 0.32), and the per-edition t-test vs zero fails
  (t = -1.94, p = 0.068). The signal is directional but not robust.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** World Cups occur every 4 years for ~5 weeks: you
  cannot build a systematic strategy around them. No meaningful capacity or
  liquidity effect. The out-of-market opportunity cost is real.
- **Confirmed?** The macro-crisis confound is the decisive issue — the World
  Cup summer effect is most plausibly a coincidence between tournament timing
  and known equity sell-offs, not sentiment from football attention.
